silo_relevance: This paper is directly relevant to derivative_pricing because it implements and benchmarks Quantum Amplitude Estimation for European option pricing, the core pricing task in this silo. Its main value is showing how QAE behaves on a concrete payoff-valuation problem, while also identifying discretization, state-preparation, and hardware-noise barriers that determine whether quantum pricing can become practical.

key_points.point: End-to-end QAE option-pricing workflow is explicitly instantiated for European derivatives.
key_points.silo_note: For derivative_pricing, the key contribution is not generic quantum computing but a full pricing pipeline: discretized terminal prices, payoff marking for in-the-money states, and conversion of amplitude into an option price.

key_points.point: The paper validates the expected O(1/ε) scaling on a pricing task, which is the central theoretical appeal of QAE for derivative valuation.
key_points.silo_note: This matters because derivative_pricing is one of the main settings where QAE is supposed to outperform classical Monte Carlo in accuracy-vs-samples scaling.

key_points.point: Discretization error is shown to be the dominant accuracy bottleneck for option pricing at feasible qubit counts.
key_points.silo_note: For derivative_pricing, payoff accuracy depends heavily on how the terminal asset distribution is discretized; the paper shows this error can dominate the pricing result even when QAE scaling is ideal.

key_points.point: The quantum pricing results are still far from practical advantage versus classical Monte Carlo for the tested derivative.
key_points.silo_note: This is crucial for derivative_pricing because it shows that, for a concrete option price benchmark, the quantum estimate remains much noisier than a standard classical pricing baseline.

key_points.point: The main implementation caveats for derivative pricing are state-preparation overhead, circuit fidelity, and the qubit gap to production accuracy.
key_points.silo_note: These limitations directly affect whether quantum option pricing can be deployed for real derivative valuation workflows, since they can erase the asymptotic benefit or require more qubits and error mitigation than currently available.

_r1_caveat: Two paper-stated caveats should be carried explicitly in prose (not just in supporting codes): (a) state preparation is excluded from the complexity analysis and 'may require O(2^n) classical preprocessing, potentially negating quantum advantage' (PDF L536-539); (b) the QAE-vs-MC comparison is against BASIC Monte Carlo only - the paper notes that 'advanced techniques (importance sampling, quasi-MC) reduce classical sample requirements by 10-100x' (PDF L547-549). Both reinforce AT-DP-001 (conditional speedup paradox) and AT-DP-004 (validation-deployment cliff).
